deal_channels.overview: Six channels for sourcing deals - from a broker network to knocking on doors.
deal_channels.description: A mix of modern channels (broker network, social media) and traditional ones (door to door, flyers), plus the skill that converts them into deals - negotiation.

personal_brokers.title: Personal agents
personal_brokers.overview: A small group of agents who understand the investment metrics and bring you a steady deal flow.
personal_brokers.description: The goal is not many agents but a small group who genuinely know what they are doing and understand the investment metrics - people who can grasp what you are actually looking for.
key_points: Their job is to build a steady deal flow that passes through you regularly
Skip the opening small talk and start with a check: does the agent know what a cap rate is
Be as specific as possible about criteria - districts, budget, required yield
You do not want agents flooding you with unsuitable listings that waste their time and yours
If you want to work with the best agents, you must be disciplined and reliable yourself - reply to offers and give direction
personal_brokers.example: For Sofia, using the 50% rule for quick analysis, the agent must know that you require a minimum 3% cap rate and aim to buy at no more than 70% of value. As long as the offer meets those criteria, the odds you act are very high.

social_networks.title: The power of social media
social_networks.overview: Attention is the new gold of the 21st century.
social_networks.description: All of people's attention is on social media. The new gold of the 21st century is not gold or cash but attention - and alongside it, trust.
key_points: If you hold people's attention and trust, the money comes to you
You must present an opportunity with visible logic for why they should follow you
In the property market there are plenty of Facebook pages where property deals are shared
social_networks.example: If you look deliberately, you will find groups and pages through which real deals pass before they ever reach the big portals.

negotiation_basics.title: Negotiation basics
negotiation_basics.overview: Price anchoring, mirroring, concessions, power and emotional control.
negotiation_basics.description: Mastering negotiation requires practice, patience and a willingness to adapt. The aim is to achieve your goals while building strong, lasting relationships.
key_points: Price anchoring: a lower opening anchor gives you room to raise and still land in a favourable position
Building rapport: finding common ground, empathy, active listening
The mirroring technique - repeating the last few words of the other side, which shows you are listening and understanding
Clear and assertive communication: be honest about your needs but open to the other side's perspective
Concessions are compromises - trading one benefit for another
Where power is unequal, emphasise the value you bring, seek allies and cite a comparable property that sold for far less
Be ready to walk away if the terms do not meet your criteria
Emotional control: avoid personal attacks, stay calm
If agreement is reached, summarise the main points and confirm each side's understanding
negotiation_basics.example: If a property is worth EUR 120,000, offer EUR 70,000 or EUR 80,000. That sets a very low anchor, and as you raise from there it looks like you are conceding - while in fact you are doing exactly what gets you the better deal.

active_deal_hunting.title: Active deal hunting
active_deal_hunting.overview: Traditional methods still carry real value - plus one aggressive tactic.
active_deal_hunting.description: Although online marketing and listings keep growing, traditional methods such as door knocking and flyer distribution retain their value. Applied creatively they expand your network and uncover untapped opportunities.
key_points: What price works for you? 70% of the property's real value
If you find a property at that price, do not hesitate - act immediately
A 'shadow offer' tactic: ask two or three friends to call with far lower offers over the course of a week, after which you offer more than theirs but still below real value
Spread the calls over days rather than one day - unless the property was just listed and the deal is attractive
This tactic works for properties listed close to their real value
active_deal_hunting.example: Warren Buffett's golden rule: investing is not like baseball - you have far more than three strikes before you are out. There is nothing to worry about even if you miss a few deals. The biggest mistakes happen in haste and in panic buying without proper analysis.

door_to_door.title: Door to door techniques
door_to_door.overview: Targeted research, a personalised approach and value-added information.
door_to_door.description: Before starting a campaign it is essential to research the target neighbourhood thoroughly - the local market, recent sales, property values, demographics and current projects.
key_points: Research helps you identify high-potential areas and narrow your target audience
A personalised approach: introduce yourself, show genuine interest and explain the purpose of your visit clearly
Tailor your pitch to the specific needs or concerns of the owners
Demonstrating knowledge of the local market builds trust
Value-added information: provide current market data, recent sales in the area and information about upcoming projects that could negatively affect value
door_to_door.example: By positioning yourself as a source of useful information rather than yet another buyer, you increase the chance of finding motivated sellers.

flyer_campaigns.title: Flyer distribution strategies
flyer_campaigns.overview: A traditional channel with surviving potential when applied creatively.
flyer_campaigns.description: Part of the same set of traditional methods - suited to expanding your network, uncovering untapped opportunities and building connections with potential buyers and sellers outside the online channels.
key_points: It works in combination with prior neighbourhood research
The goal is the same as door to door: reaching owners who have not yet listed
Off-market deals are where competition is lowest
flyer_campaigns.example: Combining flyers with personal visits in a pre-analysed neighbourhood gives access to offers that never reach the public portals.

swot_analysis.title: SWOT analysis of real estate deals
swot_analysis.overview: A strategic planning tool applied to a specific property deal.
swot_analysis.description: A thorough SWOT analysis is decisive for assessing the viability of any investment deal - long term or short term. By carefully examining strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats you can judge whether the property matches your goals and risk tolerance.
key_points: Overestimating the potential resale value leads to direct losses or lower-than-expected profit
Underestimating renovation costs is the second grossest mistake in flipping
Building a relationship with a reliable general contractor brings discounts on labour and materials

blocks.title: Opportunities
items: Market timing - buying in a rising market or one with low inventory leads to higher resale values and shorter holding periods
Developing industry expertise - relationships with contractors and agents lead to more efficient processes, lower costs and access to off-market deals

blocks.title: Threats
items: Market downturns - a property bought at the peak can lose value before the renovation is complete
Regulatory changes - changes to building codes, zoning rules or permitting can delay works and raise costs
Unforeseen problems - structural damage, mould or pest infestations extend timelines and increase costs

due_diligence.title: Due diligence. Legal, technical and financial analysis
due_diligence.overview: The process by which you protect yourself - before you sign, not after.
due_diligence.description: Once you find a property at an investment price, never jump straight into the deal. You must establish every fact about the property that is not yet known to you before signing a final contract. It is amateurish to enter an apparently attractive deal and only discover the problems after acquisition.
key_points: Nearly every step requires a paid specialist - add those amounts to your cost base and factor them into your offer
Sacrificing due diligence to cut costs is an amateur approach
The point of due diligence is not extra burden but avoiding far more serious trouble later
The outcome is one of three: you escape a bad deal, you resolve the issues in time, or you confirm there are no hidden traps

when_to_run_dd.title: When should I run due diligence?
when_to_run_dd.overview: Before the final contract - and with a mechanism that protects your deposit.
when_to_run_dd.description: Your protection must begin before acquisition. The practical solution is to set the conditions in a deposit receipt and run the checks within that window.
key_points: You set the conditions under which you will acquire the property
If problems with documentation or encumbrances emerge, the deposit amount must be returned
The only exception is if you decide to deal with the issue anyway
when_to_run_dd.example: A deposit receipt with clear conditions buys you the time to run the checks without losing the deal - and without risking the deposit.

legal_analysis.title: Legal analysis
legal_analysis.overview: Two key checks: is the seller the true owner and is the property free of encumbrances.
legal_analysis.description: The first aspect of due diligence. It requires an attorney - which in practice makes an attorney a mandatory member of your team, because without one it is hard to obtain all the necessary information. Legal analysis has the potential to uncover many treacherous traps.
key_points: Check 1 - ownership: research covering at least the previous 10 years; who owned the property, on what terms, whether all legal transactions are valid, whether claims were filed
Check 2 - encumbrances: is there a mortgage, are there seizures arising from the seller's debts, are there claims from third parties
A seizure certificate is issued by the Property Register at the Registry Agency
A mortgage continues to burden the property even after a change of ownership
For investment land, the urban planning status is reviewed - what may be built and the key construction parameters under the General Development Plan and the Spatial Planning Act
For off-plan property, the building permit, the approved architectural design and the use permit / commissioning certificate are reviewed
legal_analysis.example: As an investor hunting for attractive deals you will frequently encounter properties with documentary irregularities or debts - precisely because sellers are pressed by circumstance and therefore accept a lower price. Let regular buyers run from such deals; you must be ready to solve them.

technical_analysis.title: Technical analysis
technical_analysis.overview: The physical condition of the property and its compliance with building rules.
technical_analysis.description: The second part of due diligence - verifying whether the building and the property comply with the building codes and paperwork, and what the real technical condition is.
key_points: Verification of the construction documents and the match between what was built and the approved designs
For planned improvements (for example a pool in the yard of a house), the documentation is reviewed to see whether such an improvement is permitted at all
Hidden technical problems are among the main threats in a flipping SWOT analysis
technical_analysis.example: You want a house with a large yard and plan to add a pool - the relevant documentation must be reviewed in advance to know whether the improvement is allowed.

financial_analysis.title: Financial analysis
financial_analysis.overview: The full picture of income, expenses and liabilities attached to the property.
financial_analysis.description: The third aspect of due diligence, where an accountant is useful - verifying every financial circumstance around the property and calculating whether the deal works on real rather than presented numbers.
key_points: The cost of the analyses themselves also belongs in the cost base of the deal
Often a deposit paid on a preliminary contract goes toward clearing debts attached to the property, because the owner is insolvent
Working through complex deals brings invaluable experience that pays off later
financial_analysis.example: If your deposit effectively goes toward repaying the seller's debts, that must be clear, documented and calculated before signing.

contract_terms.title: Contract terms
contract_terms.overview: Why an understated price in the title deed is a trap, not a saving.
contract_terms.description: The closing part covers what goes into the documents and the consequences of attempting to 'optimise' through under-the-table payments.
key_points: In an eviction (judicial removal in favour of a third true owner) you can only claim the amount stated in the title deed
Anything paid 'under the table' is not recoverable
In the title deed you declare that the stated price is the actual one; if that is untrue you bear criminal liability under Art. 313 of the Criminal Code
So you neither recover the real amount nor escape criminal liability
contract_terms.example: The question 'are the saved taxes and fees worth it now?' has one unambiguous answer: no.

financing.title: Financing real estate investments
financing.overview: Mortgage lending in depth, the alternative instruments and every cost in the transaction.
financing.description: In a large share of deals investors use other people's money. Since 95% of externally financed transactions in Bulgaria run through a bank mortgage, that is the method carrying the most weight, followed by the alternatives common in more developed markets.
key_points: In Bulgaria financing is offered on identical terms to everyone - there are no products tailored to investors
In developed markets there are BTL ('buy to let') loans with investor-specific terms
The market is the way it is because of its youth and the consequences of the mistakes exposed in 2008

mortgage_lending.title: Mortgage lending
mortgage_lending.overview: The cheapest and most preferred way to finance a purchase in Bulgaria.
mortgage_lending.description: A mortgage loan is a bank loan secured against property. The security means the pledged property backs the financing, and if servicing stops the lender has the right to take it. Every mortgage in Bulgaria is created in notarised form.
key_points: Most common term: between 15 and 30 years
35 years is the upper limit in Bulgaria, and few banks will go there
Banks typically lend 80-90% of the property price
In the USA 40-year mortgages are now appearing because of growing affordability pressure

mortgage_types.title: Types of mortgage loans
mortgage_types.overview: Purpose-bound versus unrestricted, contractual versus statutory mortgage.
mortgage_types.description: The main split is by the intended use of the funds, and within purpose-bound loans by how the mortgage is created, which directly affects the notary fee.
key_points: Unrestricted mortgages - a type of consumer loan with no requirements on how the money is used; higher interest, but better terms than an unsecured consumer loan
An investor uses only purpose-bound loans - your intentions must be transparent and you need the better terms
Banks love predictability - that is exactly what justifies better terms
Purpose-bound mortgages split into contractual and statutory
With a statutory mortgage the entire amount goes to the seller - the sole purpose is the purchase; the notary fee is lower
With a contractual mortgage part of the amount goes elsewhere, which makes it contractual and the fee higher
If a property other than the one being bought is pledged, the mortgage is always contractual
mortgage_types.example:
You borrow EUR 70,000 and the whole amount goes to the seller - a statutory mortgage. You borrow EUR 70,000 but EUR 65,000 goes to the seller and the remainder elsewhere - a contractual mortgage and a higher notary fee.

During the 2008 crisis there were plenty of bad loans taken by imprudent clients who drew unrestricted mortgage loans they eventually could not service.

interest_rate_types.title: Types of interest - fixed and floating
interest_rate_types.overview: How the floating rate is formed and why fixed rates in Bulgaria are capped at 5 years.
interest_rate_types.description: The floating rate consists of a variable component (the reference rate) and a fixed margin. The contract describes the methodology for applying the reference rate with a clear calculation procedure specifying the quantities, type and relative weight of components such as market indices and indicators.
key_points: The methodology written into the contract cannot be changed unilaterally by the lender
Each bank chooses how to form the floating component - which creates competitive differences in terms
Until around the end of 2021 Bulgaria offered fixing for long periods or the whole term - no longer
Banks currently offer a maximum of 5 years fixed (other common options are 1 and 3 years), after which it becomes floating
The reason: it is hard for banks to make economic forecasts beyond 5 years
The floating rate carries risk: if central banks raise policy rates it can rise significantly and even exceed fixed offerings
Always account for interest rate risk - every change in the cost base affects the investment
interest_rate_types.example: As of 2023, leading credit consultants estimate that close to 65% of Bulgarians choose floating-rate mortgages and 35% fixed. The latter expect sharp rate rises and want a period of predictability.

installment_types.title: Types of mortgage instalments
installment_types.description: Three repayment schemes, each suited to a different situation.
key_points: Annuity - equal in size; early on they contain more interest and less principal, with the ratio reversing over time. The most common type
Decreasing - an equal monthly amount of principal plus interest on the remaining balance; each instalment is smaller than the last
Grace period - for a set period you pay only the interest due, with no principal
installment_types.example: Grace-period instalments are negotiated when renovation or reconfiguration is needed: they reduce costs in the first months, and by the time full payments begin the property has already started producing rental income.

the_best_loan.title: Which is the most favourable loan?
the_best_loan.overview: There is no universal answer - only criteria, different for every investor.
the_best_loan.description: Any consultant will tell you no such thing exists, because everything is defined by the requirements of the specific investor, and those are never identical. A low rate is far from the only condition.
key_points: One investor wants the lowest APR and interest rate
Another wants a minimal payment through the longest possible term - in Bulgaria the maximum is 35 years, but as of 2023 few banks will go there; the common ceiling is 30 years
A third wants the loan approved as fast as possible to capture a good deal - here what matters is which bank can halve the standard 30-day approval
A fourth wants minimal own contribution and maximum financing
There is no universal formula for ranking loans from best to worst
the_best_loan.example: If your deal is competitive and you must be first, a bank that approves in 15 days at a slightly higher rate beats one with the lowest rate and a 30-day process.

early_repayment.title: Save interest through early repayment
early_repayment.overview: When and how early repayment genuinely saves money.
early_repayment.description: If you decide to sharply reduce the outstanding amount on an existing loan, you can make a full or partial early repayment. This is exactly where you can save on interest.
key_points: The effect is strongest with annuity instalments - the most standard type
The penalty fee for early repayment usually applies only in the first period; after that there is none
For partial early repayment you must have at least 6 monthly instalments ready
The bank amends your repayment schedule
That amendment is usually free once a year
More frequent requests trigger fees - plan your actions and do not repay more than once a year
early_repayment.example: If you accumulate funds for partial repayment twice in a year, it is smarter to combine them into one payment so you use the free schedule amendment.

refinancing.title: Refinancing and loan management
refinancing.overview: A loan is not a one-time decision - it is managed.
refinancing.description: Since every bank sets its own floating component, some offer better terms as part of a more aggressive client acquisition policy. That creates opportunities for the borrower even after a contract has been signed.
key_points: Refinancing replaces an existing loan with a new one on better terms
The goals can be saving money, reducing monthly payments or obtaining better loan terms
It can also be used to buy a new property - this is the mechanism at the heart of the BRRRR strategy
Keep watching the market after signing - competition between banks works in your favour
refinancing.example: Refinancing is exactly what turns a one-off purchase into a repeating cycle: you recover your invested capital and direct it into the next property.

currency_risk.title: Currency risk
currency_risk.overview: The Swiss franc episode as a warning.
currency_risk.description: A classic example of risk that does not appear in the initial calculations. Borrowers ended up trapped: the payment rose because of the currency while the collateral devalued because of the burst property bubble.
key_points: Does it make sense to service a loan that keeps growing on a property losing value? Yet if you stop, the collateral does not cover the debt and you remain a debtor
The situation was also unfavourable for the banks, which risked a large volume of bad loans with devalued collateral
Some borrowers negotiated lower rates, others conversion into levs
An agreement was reached between the Consumer Protection Commission and one of the three banks: the increase is split 80:20
Many people went to court arguing the contracts lacked clauses explaining currency risk and contained unfair terms
Such offers no longer exist in Bulgaria - deals are in euro and the lev is pegged to the euro at a fixed rate, so there is no currency risk
currency_risk.example:
Under the 80:20 scheme, a loan increase of BGN 50,000 means BGN 40,000 is covered by the bank and BGN 10,000 remains with the borrower.

In Hungary and Poland, Swiss franc mortgages made up close to 40-50% of all loans in the years before the financial crisis, forcing state intervention - in Hungary the so-called 'Orbanomics' relief scheme, largely paid for by the banks.

Tip: use loan calculators to 'stress test' different scenarios - periods of negative cash flow or rate increases.

alternative_financing.title: Alternative financing options
alternative_financing.overview: Hard money loans and private lenders - standard in more developed markets.
alternative_financing.description: Although 95% of financing in Bulgaria runs through banks, alternative instruments are common in more developed markets. Hard money loans are short-term, asset-based loans provided by private lenders rather than banks or credit unions.
key_points: The main difference from conventional loans lies in the underwriting process
Lenders focus on the value of the collateral rather than the borrower's creditworthiness, income or DTI
They provide fast access to funds, but at higher interest rates and fees because of the elevated risk
They are used for property investments, business expansion and other situations requiring short-term financing
They allow borrowers who cannot qualify for traditional financing to act
Limitations: higher rates and fees, short terms and the possibility of losing the property

bridge_loans.title: Bridge loans
bridge_loans.overview: Short-term financing that covers the gap between two transactions.
bridge_loans.description: The first type of hard money loan - a short-term instrument for the moment when your funds are locked in one property while the next opportunity requires capital now.
key_points: Approval rests on the value of the collateral rather than the credit profile
Fast access to funds at a higher cost of capital
Suitable for time-sensitive deals
bridge_loans.example: A bridge loan lets you acquire a new property before realising the current one, instead of missing the opportunity.

fix_and_flip_loans.title: Fix and flip loans
fix_and_flip_loans.overview: A product built specifically for fix and flip investors.
fix_and_flip_loans.description: Designed for investors who buy properties, renovate them and then sell at a profit. They provide funds for the purchase, the renovation costs and even the carrying costs during the rehab process.
key_points: They cover all three cost categories of a flip at once
The cost of capital is higher, but the time frame is short
They enable work on distressed properties a bank would not finance
fix_and_flip_loans.example: An investor finds a distressed property in an up-and-coming neighbourhood with a purchase price of EUR 100,000, needing further funds for renovation before it can be sold.

construction_loans.title: Construction loans
construction_loans.description: A type of hard money loan aimed at projects where value is created through building rather than through buying an existing asset.
key_points: The collateral is the project and the land beneath it
Short terms aligned with the construction stages
Exit from the loan: selling the finished units or refinancing with a conventional loan
construction_loans.example: A construction loan covers the build, and repayment comes from the sale of the completed units.

land_loans.title: Land loans
land_loans.description: They allow the acquisition of land that traditional lenders usually avoid, secured against the plot itself.
key_points: Suitable when planning to subdivide or develop
Repayment comes from selling the plots or the built units
Higher risk and therefore a higher cost of capital
land_loans.example: An investor identifies a 10-acre plot with development potential, secures a land loan to buy it and plans to subdivide and build several single-family homes. After construction they sell the individual plots or houses to repay the loan and take a profit.

owner_occupied_loans.title: Owner-occupied loans
owner_occupied_loans.overview: Hard money for people who will live in the property.
owner_occupied_loans.description: Although hard money loans target investors and developers, some lenders offer loans to owners who plan to live in the property they buy.
key_points: Used by borrowers who cannot qualify for traditional financing due to poor credit, a recent bankruptcy or other financial challenges
Usually short term
They require the borrower to refinance with a conventional loan or sell the property within a set period
owner_occupied_loans.example: A borrower with a recent bankruptcy does not qualify for a traditional mortgage but obtains a hard money loan to buy a home. They then work on improving their credit position in order to refinance conventionally or sell within the loan term.

private_money_lenders.title: Private money lenders
private_money_lenders.overview: An alternative when traditional institutions have overly strict criteria.
private_money_lenders.description: Investors often need alternative financing solutions because traditional financial institutions can impose strict criteria that limit their access to capital. Private lenders offer flexible loan products and personalised service.
key_points: Understanding the different hard money loan types - bridge, fix and flip, construction, land, refinance and cash-out, owner-occupied - allows an informed choice
Hard money loans are a valuable tool for investors, developers and owners seeking flexible, fast financing
It is essential to weigh the benefits and drawbacks - they are not suitable for every borrower or project
private_money_lenders.example: When the emphasis is on collateral value rather than creditworthiness, opportunities open for borrowers a bank would refuse.

working_with_private_lenders.title: Understanding private lenders for real estate investors
working_with_private_lenders.overview: Who they are, what the advantages are and how to work with them.
working_with_private_lenders.description: Private lenders are non-institutional entities providing loans to individuals and legal entities. They can be individuals, groups or, rarely, companies with access to a substantial capital pool. They are often specialised in specific industries or loan products.
key_points: 1. Flexibility - often more flexible lending criteria than traditional institutions; more willing to approve investors with unusual financial situations or non-traditional income sources
2. Speed - approval is usually faster than with banks, which can be decisive for time-sensitive property investments
3. Customisation - they adapt products to specific needs: interest-only payments, longer repayment periods
4. Relationship-based lending - the long-term relationship is part of the product itself
working_with_private_lenders.example: For an investor with a non-standard income profile but a strong deal, a private lender may be the only route to financing within the required timeframe.

transaction_costs.title: Additional costs in a property purchase transaction
transaction_costs.overview: All the costs that must enter your calculation - otherwise the analysis is wrong.
transaction_costs.description: You cannot assess the potential of your investment without knowing exactly what it will cost. The costs of a transaction - with or without a mortgage - are not small, and miscalculating them is a gross mistake to avoid at all costs.
key_points: These three costs are due whether you buy with a mortgage or with your own funds
With a mortgage, further costs related to the loan and the creation of the mortgage are added
A specific case may involve something extra, but the listed items cover the vast majority of the cost base
transaction_costs.example: On a EUR 100,000 purchase in Sofia the local tax alone is EUR 3,000, plus EUR 100 in registration fees, plus notary fees - costs that must be in the calculation before you decide whether the price is an investment price.

blocks.title: Mandatory costs
items: Municipal/local tax (property acquisition tax) - the largest additional cost, set by the municipality where the deal takes place: a floor of 0.1% and a ceiling of 3%. In Sofia it is 3%. Each municipality sets and may change this rate itself
Registration fee to the Registry Agency - 0.10% of the transaction value

Notary fees - depending on the certified material interest and any additional services; see point 8 of the Notary Fees Tariff. Payment varies because of Bulgarian notary practices (avoiding the double fee, offering free services to attract clients), so it is best to consult

glossary.title: Key terms
glossary.overview: A glossary of the core concepts in property investing.
glossary.description: A closing reference section with definitions of the main terms in property investing - from basic roles to financial metrics and strategies.

glossary.definition: A licensed professional who facilitates the purchase, sale or letting of property on behalf of clients; an intermediary between buyers and sellers.
A loan taken to finance the purchase of a property, where the property itself serves as collateral; repaid over time, usually with interest.
The use of borrowed funds (for example a mortgage) to finance a property investment.
Replacing an existing loan with a new one on better terms - to save money, reduce payments or buy a new property.
A general rise in the price level over a period; it measures the decline in the purchasing power of the currency.
A strategy to offset or reduce the risk of potential losses from adverse price movements.
An increase in a property's value over time, driven by market conditions and other factors.
Raising value through your own deliberate actions - improvements and renovation - rather than through market movement.
An accounting method for allocating the cost of tangible assets over time; in real estate, a non-cash expense with a tax effect.
A company that owns, operates or finances income-producing real estate and distributes at least 90% of its taxable income as dividends.
The Bulgarian term for a REIT - a joint-stock company with a special investment purpose.
The percentage of vacant (unlet) properties or units in the portfolio.
A financial metric: property price / annual gross rent.
The amount remaining after deducting all expenses, including mortgage, taxes and insurance.
The difference between the market value of the property and the outstanding mortgage balance.
The income generated by a property after operating expenses but before debt payments.
Spending on significant improvements, repairs or replacements to maintain the property.
A measure of the annual return relative to the equity actually invested.
A core metric in property investment analysis: NOI / acquisition price.
A method of raising capital by pooling funds from multiple investors.
A strategy where an underpriced property is put under contract and the rights under it are resold to an end buyer.
An acronym for 'buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat'.
A metric lenders use to assess a borrower's ability to service debt.
A metric lenders use to assess loan risk relative to the value of the collateral.
A strategy of buying, renovating and quickly reselling a property at a profit.
The reference rate against which other interest rates in the economy are set.
A strategic planning tool: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.
